statement: The supplied sources genuinely contain nothing to derive, as no mathematical derivation of a feedback loop is provided. A feedback loop is defined as a closed-loop system configuration formed when all or some portion of the output of a system, process, or device is routed back, sampled, and applied as an input as part of a chain of cause and effect; in an amplifier where the fed-back signal is subtracted from the input, the loop gain around the loop is defined by the product $-AB$, where $A$ is the open-loop gain and $B$ is the feedback network gain.

symbols.meaning: loop gain around the feedback loop with subtractive feedback
angular frequency of the input signal

properties.property: In a feedback amplifier with subtractive feedback, the loop gain is the product of the amplifier gain and feedback network gain, $-AB$.
properties.why: loop gain is the product of all gains around the loop with a minus sign representing subtraction at the input

properties.property: Negative feedback occurs when the fed-back signal is out of phase by 180° with respect to the input signal, reducing gain and increasing stability and accuracy.
properties.why: subtractive out-of-phase feedback counteracts errors and desensitizes the system to unwanted fluctuations

properties.property: Positive feedback occurs when the fed-back signal is in phase with the input signal, increasing amplifier gain and reinforcing the input.
properties.why: in-phase feedback reinforces the input signal under sufficient gain conditions

properties.property: On a decibel scale, amplifier loop gain equals the difference between the open-loop gain curve and the closed-loop gain curve (1/B curve).
properties.why: gains vary with angular frequency $\omega$ and subtraction in decibels represents the ratio of gains

properties.property: A device operates in closed loop when output feedback is employed, and in open loop when no output feedback is employed.
properties.why: a feedback loop is created only when all or some portion of the output is routed back to the input

assumptions.assumption: The system response time is sufficiently fast relative to changes in the input signal.
assumptions.breaks_when: The input changes faster than the system can respond, creating phase lag in the arrival of the corrective signal.

assumptions.assumption: The feedback system can be analyzed as isolated loops without unmodeled cross-coupling.
assumptions.breaks_when: The number of interacting parts increases such that mutual cross-couplings generate numerous intertwined circuits whose individual properties do not determine the whole system's behavior.

assumptions.assumption: Loop gain and phase shift remain within stability boundaries across operational frequencies.
assumptions.breaks_when: Loop gain is sufficient in the presence of in-phase feedback or 180° response lag, leading to instability or oscillation.

failure_modes.signature: The system output oscillates or hunts continuously around the target value rather than settling.
failure_modes.cause: The input changes faster than the system can respond, causing lag in the arrival of the corrective feedback signal.

failure_modes.signature: The output becomes locked or frozen at its maximum or minimum operational limit.
failure_modes.cause: Positive feedback reinforces the signal until the device reaches and locks into a saturation state.

failure_modes.signature: Loud, sustained squeal or howl emitted at the maximum power capability of the amplifier.
failure_modes.cause: A microphone picks up the acoustic output from a connected loudspeaker and re-amplifies it with sufficient loop gain.

failure_modes.mode: Disruption of tissue integrity and immune coordination
failure_modes.signature: Loss of tissue architecture and failure of coordinated cellular immune response.
failure_modes.cause: Failure of cellular and molecular feedback interactions mediated by adhesion and signaling molecules (such as in cancer).
